deep.reconstruction:
CONTEXT. The page belongs to a sequence of folios in which the elements of an orbit are corrected from opposition observations. The quantities fit Ceres: φ≈4°29.6' (e=sinφ≈0.0783), node ≈80°53', inclination ≈10°37', perihelion ≈146°40', daily motion ≈770.9", log a=0.44207. This folio treats the 5th opposition, almost certainly that of 1805. It then combines the five opposition equations of condition (I–V) to obtain corrections to the elements.

(A) MEAN MOTION AND SECULAR VARIATIONS (left column).
- log t = 3.2898462, so t ≈ 1949.2 days from the epoch. log n = 2.8869746, so n ≈ 770.86"/day.
- log(n t) = 6.1768208, so n t = 1502522.10" = 417°22'2.10" of mean motion.
- The same t multiplied by the rates with logs 9.52135, 7.51655, 7.60763, 7.07941 gives 647.43", 6.40", 7.90", 2.34".
- These match the yearly rates tabulated on the next page: perihelion +121.2"/yr, φ −1.2"/yr, node +1.48"/yr, inclination −0.44"/yr.
- They give the elements valid at opposition V: perihelion π = 146°40'41.19", φ = 4°29'35.55", Ω = 80°53'25.19".

(B) PERTURBATION.
- The block 294°38'8.0", 10°14'15.4", 304°52'23.4", 212°51'30.7", 267°59'7.3" forms a mean-longitude difference: 267°59'7.3" = 212°51'30.7" − 304°52'23.4" (mod 360°).
- Multiples of this argument (118°11½', 323°7', 113°7', 231°6') feed series terms −43457, 47733, 94240, 99497, +3493.3, −816.4, +2676.9.
- The two terms +305.23" and +865.70" sum exactly to 1170.93" = +19'30.93". This is the correction added to the computed orbit longitude below.
- The same numbers (+15'45.01", +9'4.25", −4'45.45", +12'34.44", +19'30.93" for I–V) reappear on the neighbouring pages. My interpretation (not stated on the page): it is a periodic perturbation in longitude, most plausibly by Jupiter.

(C) POSITION AT OPPOSITION V (centre column).
- Mean longitude: L = 155°29'28.57" + 417°22'2.10" = 212°51'30.67" (mod 360°).
- Mean anomaly: M = L − π = 66°10'49.48".
- Kepler's equation by iteration, using e in seconds (log eρ = log sinφ + log ρ = 8.8939887 + 5.3144251 = 4.2084138, i.e. eρ = 16158.6"): E = M + eρ sinE gives +4°13'43.55" and E = 70°24'33.03".
- True anomaly: v − E = +4°17'22.99", computed from auxiliary logs (log sin E = 9.9741024, log sin(φ/2) = 8.5932926, …). This is equivalent to tan(v/2) = √((1+e)/(1−e)) tan(E/2) and gives v = 74°41'56.02".
- Other auxiliary logs: log cos v = 9.42143, log cos E = 9.5254345, log(1 − e cosE) = 9.98844, log a = 0.4420728.
- Orbit longitude: v + π = 221°22'37.21". Adding the perturbation +19'30.93" gives 221°42'8.14".
- Equation of condition, with corrections E (epoch/mean longitude), ω (perihelion), φ (eccentricity angle), μ (daily motion):
  l = 221°42'8.14" + 2049.4μ − 0.05143ω + 1.05143E + 1.9550φ.
- Here 1.05143 = (1 + e cos v)²/(1 − e²)^{3/2} = dv/dM. The ω-coefficient is 1 − dv/dM. 2049.4 = t·dv/dM. 1.9550 = sin v (2 + e cos v)/(1 − e²)·cos φ = dv/dφ. Note E + ω coefficients sum to 1, which is why later equations use (ω − E).

(D) OBSERVED HELIOCENTRIC PLACE REDUCED TO THE ORBIT (right columns).
- Observed heliocentric ecliptic longitude: 222°14'9.10".
- l − Ω = 141°20'43.91", with log tan = 9.9030070 and log cos i = 9.9924883.
- tan u = tan(l − Ω)/cos i gives u = 140°51'40.47", so the orbit longitude is u + Ω = 221°45'5.66".
- Latitude: tan β = tan i·sin(l − Ω), using log sin(l − Ω) = 9.7956174 and log tan i = 9.2732610, gives β = 6°41'1.75".
- Compared with 221°42'8.14" this gives the absolute term of equation V.
- A rough check at the bottom right repeats the reduction: 221°41'8" − 80°53'25" gives 141°17'46" in the ecliptic, i.e. 222°11'11".
- The small columns give logs of the E-coefficients: 9.99866 − 9.97688 = 0.02178 = log 1.05143. Also 1.993856 and 0.026268 (= e cosE ≈ 0.02627).

(E) FIRST SOLUTION (middle block).
- Gauss eliminates successively on the five equations, written with unknowns E, μ, φ, (ω − E):
  - Normalised first equation: E + 1034.59μ + 0.3597φ − 0.02445(ω − E) − 34.086 = 0. It removes E from four others.
  - φ + 92.53μ + 0.010075(ω − E) − 44.48 = 0 removes φ from three.
  - (ω − E) − 1848.9μ + 57.39 = 0 leaves two equations in μ alone: −954.3μ + 140.00 and −2045.2μ + 118.33.
- He adopts μ = 0.076988 (log 8.88642), with "bleibt 33.04" (residual).
- Back-substitution: ω − E = 84.95, φ = +36.50", E = −56.62", ω = +28.33". I verified these are mutually consistent.

(F) SECOND SOLUTION ("Hieraus wurden folgende Gleichungen abgeleitet").
- An upper-triangular reduced system, in the form of Gauss's elimination of normal equations, with a final remainder "bleibt 61.866" (log 9.70519):
  - 4.60893E + 4649.31μ + 1.62336φ − 0.31202ω − 155.124 = 0
  - 2392.72μ − 0.01905φ + 0.080079ω − 161.924 = 0
  - 20.4896φ − 0.62083ω − 386.969 = 0
  - 1.35366ω − 495.257 = 0
- Back-substitution with logarithms:
  - log ω = 2.69483 − 0.13151 = 2.56332, so ω = +365.87". A first attempt, 444.96, is struck out together with its products 276.240, 35.632, 138.835.
  - 0.62083ω = 227.140, so 20.4896φ = 614.109 and φ = +29.976".
  - 0.01905φ = 0.571 and 0.080079ω = 29.298, so 2392.72μ = 133.197, log μ = 2.12449 − 3.37889 = 8.74560 and 1000μ = 55.6675".
  - 4649.31μ = 258.82, 1.62336φ = 48.661, 0.31202ω = 114.155, so 4.60893E = −38.202 and E = −8.29".
- The large crossed-out X contains an abandoned earlier back-substitution (constants 269.77, 152.626, E = −8.80", +29.41").
errors: Last-digit slips in the logarithms. log 614.109 = 2.788245 but Gauss uses 2.78830, giving φ = 29.976 instead of 29.972. log 4.60893 = 0.663600 but Gauss writes 0.66354. Effects ≤0.005", negligible.
log sin(φ/2) is given as 8.5932926; my recomputation gives ≈8.593293, consistent. The resulting v − E = 4°17'22.99" checks to 0.1".
The first attempt ω = 444.96" in the back-substitution was wrong (495.257/1.35366 = 365.87). Gauss himself struck it out and redid the dependent products.

The way μ = 0.076988 was chosen from the two final equations of the first block (−954.3μ + 140.00, −2045.2μ + 118.33) is not evident. It is neither either single root nor their unweighted least-squares value (0.0737), so implicit weights (the log multipliers) were probably used. I could not confirm this. I also could not reproduce from the visible equations of condition how the triangular system in (F) was formed.

results.what: Mean anomaly to eccentric anomaly to true anomaly via iterated Kepler equation and the half-angle (tan φ/2 / sin φ/2) relation; heliocentric reduction to ecliptic (tan u = tan(l−Ω)/cos i, tan β = tan i sin(l−Ω)).
results.modern_name: Two-body ephemeris computation (Kepler's equation, true anomaly, reduction to the ecliptic)

results.what: Partial derivatives of true longitude with respect to the elements: dv/dM = (1+e cos v)^2/(1-e^2)^(3/2), dv/de = sin v (2+e cos v)/(1-e^2), giving linear equations of condition in corrections to epoch, perihelion, eccentricity angle and mean motion.
results.modern_name: Differential correction of orbital elements (linearized equations of condition)
results.usually_credited_to: Euler, Lagrange, Laplace; systematized by Gauss (Theoria Motus 1809)

results.what: Application of a periodic perturbation in longitude (+19'30.93" = 305.23" + 865.70") to the computed longitude, from series in multiples of a mean-longitude difference, most plausibly Jupiter acting on Ceres.
results.usually_credited_to: Lagrange/Laplace; Gauss's Ceres–Jupiter perturbations are documented in his correspondence and Werke

results.what: Solution of 5 opposition equations in 4 unknowns by successive elimination. Second version: triangular reduced system with remainder ('bleibt 61.866') and logarithmic back-substitution, consistent with Gaussian elimination of least-squares normal equations.
results.modern_name: Least squares / Gaussian elimination (Gauss's algorithm for normal equations)

deep.surprise_reason: This is routine working material from Gauss's well-documented 1805 orbit corrections for Ceres from its first five oppositions, including Jupiter perturbations and least-squares-style elimination. Gauss is already known to have done this work, and it is reflected in Theoria Motus and his correspondence with Olbers and Zach. Nothing here goes beyond what is credited to him.
